blocks.text: I can describe the formation of fossils and how the rock cycle affects our fossil record.

items.title: Forming fossils
items.sub: How a living thing becomes a fossil

items.title: The rock cycle and fossil record
items.sub: Which rocks hold fossils, and why fossils get broken

blocks.text: Tap each word to see what it means.

items.def: The mineralised remains or impression of once-living organisms, or of traces left behind by organisms (e.g. skeletons, shells or impressions).
An element or compound with a crystal-like structure. They are the 'building blocks' of rocks.
A material deposited by water, wind or ice, such as pebbles or sand.
A type of rock formed from the compression of sediments (rock fragments, minerals and remains of dead plants and animals).
The gradual recycling of rocks over millions of years.

blocks.text: Some rocks contain physical evidence of ancient life. These are called {fossils}. The word fossil comes from the Latin 'fossilis', which means 'unearthed'.
Fossils are typically more than 10 000 years old. A fossil can be:

items.title: Remains or impressions
items.sub: of an organism itself, such as a leaf impression

items.title: Traces of behaviour
items.sub: such as footprints or animal dung (coprolite)

items.title: Whole organism
items.sub: The entire organism is preserved, including its soft parts. This is the rarest type, e.g. insects trapped in amber.

items.title: Hard parts, original form
items.sub: Hard parts such as bones, shells or exoskeletons are preserved in their original chemical form. Common in young sediments, e.g. tar pits.

items.title: Hard parts, altered form
items.sub: Hard parts are preserved in an altered chemical form, because they have been mineralised. These are the most common fossils.

blocks.text: Most fossils form in a similar way to sedimentary rocks.

items: An organism dies and is quickly buried in sediment.
Decomposers break down the soft parts, leaving the hard parts.
More layers of sediment build up. This increases the pressure and makes the strata compact.
Compaction creates the conditions for mineral crystals to form.

blocks.text: The remaining hard parts of the organism are **mineralised** (altered). This can happen in two ways:

items.title: Pores fill up
items.sub: The pores in the hard parts fill with mineral-rich water, and mineral crystals grow in the pores.

items.title: Replaced by minerals
items.sub: The hard parts dissolve in the mineral-rich water and are replaced with mineral crystals from that water.

blocks.label: What is a 'stone photocopy'?
blocks.text: Mineralisation creates a 'stone photocopy' of the organism. After many thousands to millions of years, a fossil is formed.

items.q: What happens to an organism at the start of fossil formation?
options: It is quickly buried in sediment
It is heated to a high temperature underground
They break down the soft parts, leaving the hard parts
They break down the hard parts, leaving the soft parts
They turn the soft parts into minerals

items.q: Which type of fossil is the rarest?
options: Hard parts in an altered chemical form
An entire organism, including its soft parts
Hard parts in their original chemical form

items.q: A footprint left by an animal is a fossil that shows...

blocks.text: A collection of fossils documenting the history of life on Earth is called the {fossil record}.
By studying the fossil record, scientists can learn about past environments and how life has changed over time.
Less than 1% of organisms become a fossil. Special conditions are needed.

slides.title: Conditions for a fossil to form

items.title: Body type
items.sub: Organisms with hard parts are more likely to form fossils than those with soft parts.

items.title: Exposure
items.sub: The organism must be buried quickly after death. This is more likely near flowing water or wind, which erode and deposit sediment. Smaller organisms need less sediment to be buried.

items.title: Sediment type
items.sub: Acidic sediments react with calcium phosphate, the chemical that makes hard parts hard, and destroy them. Alkaline sediments do not.

blocks.q: Choose the more likely to become a fossil.

items.q: A trilobite (many hard parts) or a jellyfish (no hard parts)?
Buried in acidic sediment or in alkaline sediment?
Buried quickly after death or left uncovered?

blocks.text: Earth is dynamic, which means it is constantly changing. The crust is broken into pieces called tectonic plates. As they move, conditions in the crust and upper mantle change, and this affects the type of rock that might form.

items.title: Sedimentary
items.sub: Sediments are deposited, compacted and cemented together

items.title: Metamorphic
items.sub: Other rocks are put under intense heat and pressure

blocks.text: All types of rock undergo weathering and erosion.
Scientists use a {rock cycle} to keep track of the conditions that form each rock and the changes between them. Here are some of the processes:

items: Weathering and erosion turn any rock into sediment.
Compaction and cementation turn sediment into sedimentary rock.
Heat and pressure can turn sedimentary or igneous rock into metamorphic rock.
Melting turns metamorphic or igneous rock into magma.
Crystallisation turns magma into igneous rock.

blocks.label: Watch out!
blocks.text: A simple circle can be misleading. It wrongly suggests that one type of rock will always change into another, specific type. For example, not all sedimentary rocks form metamorphic rocks.

blocks.q: Match each process to what it produces.

blocks.text: A fossil takes many thousands of years to form, similar to a sedimentary rock. Fossils are usually found in sedimentary rocks because they are formed by a similar process.
Geological processes involving intense heat and pressure distort fossils, and melting destroys them entirely. So fossils are not found in metamorphic or igneous rocks.

Fossils can also be found incomplete or broken, for example because of weathering and erosion, extreme compaction, or sudden shifts such as earthquakes and landslides. Larger fossils are more likely to be broken.

blocks.label: Are broken fossils still useful?
blocks.text: Yes. Most fossils in the fossil record are broken or incomplete, but they still give a lot of evidence about how organisms might have died and lived, and about the conditions that scattered their remains.

blocks.q: Which type of rock could contain fossils?

items.q: Why are fossils not found in metamorphic rock?
options: Intense heat and pressure distort them

items.q: Which of these may mean a fossil is found broken?

items: Fossils are found in sedimentary rock, but not in other types of rock.
Fossils are often the remains or imprints of living plants or animals.
Bones buried in sedimentary rock can be very, very slowly dissolved by water and replaced by minerals in the water.
Geological activities can break (earthquakes), distort (intense heat and pressure) or destroy (melting) fossils.

worksheet.title: Worksheet: Fossils and the rock cycle
worksheet.instructions: Answer each question with a word, a number or a short phrase.

questions.prompt: What do we call the mineralised remains or impression of once-living organisms?
questions.explanation: Fossils are the mineralised remains or impressions of once-living organisms.

questions.prompt: Fossils are usually found in which type of rock?
questions.explanation: Fossils are formed by a similar process to sedimentary rocks and are usually found in them.

questions.prompt: A footprint shows an organism's behaviour. What kind of fossil is it?
questions.explanation: A trace fossil shows an organism's behaviour, such as footprints.

questions.prompt: Amber traps insects. Amber is fossilised what?
Which living things break down an organism's soft parts, leaving the hard parts?
questions.explanation: Decomposers break down the soft parts of a dead organism.

questions.prompt: Which chemical, found in bones, makes hard parts hard and reacts with acidic sediments?
questions.explanation: Calcium phosphate makes hard parts hard, and acidic sediments react with it.

questions.prompt: What is a collection of fossils documenting the history of life on Earth called?
questions.explanation: The fossil record documents the history of life on Earth.

questions.prompt: Less than what percentage of organisms become a fossil? Give the number only.
questions.explanation: Less than 1% of organisms become a fossil.

questions.prompt: Which type of rock forms when magma cools and crystallises?
questions.explanation: Igneous rocks form when magma cools and crystallises.

questions.prompt: Which type of rock forms when other rocks are put under intense heat and pressure?
questions.explanation: Metamorphic rocks form under intense heat and pressure.
